Open your browser's network tab — you'll see 0 bytes uploaded

Most online STL tools upload your file to a server and then promise to delete it. These tools never receive it in the first place. Every byte of parsing, rendering, and math happens on your own hardware, which is why they can make a guarantee instead of a promise: your model is confidential by default, not by policy.

How it works in three steps

  1. 1

    Open a tool and drop in your file — or pick your scales

    No sign-up, no upload dialog. The file is read straight from your disk by the page itself.

  2. 2

    The tool analyzes it locally

    Rendering, dimension math, format conversion, and mesh checks all run on your own hardware.

  3. 3

    You keep the result

    A screenshot, a converted file on your disk, or an exact percentage to type into your slicer.

A real example

A miniature exported in inches imports into a metric slicer 25.4× too small. A "close enough" 115% instead of the exact 114.3% means a twenty-model unit ends up visibly shorter than the rest of the army. These tools exist to settle that before the printer starts.

Every tool is free, and stays free. If one of them saves you a failed print,you can support the site — no pressure either way.

What can you do here without installing anything?

  • Check a downloaded model's real dimensions before you commit filament or resin to it.

  • Convert STL to OBJ or PLY for a sculpting, rendering, or CAD pipeline.

  • Find non-manifold edges before a ten-hour print, not after it.

  • Inspect a client's confidential model without routing it through someone else's cloud.

  • Open an STL on a locked-down work computer where you cannot install software.

  • Keep working offline — after the first page load, no connection is needed.

Questions people actually ask about browser STL tools

Straight answers, no marketing.

Do I need to upload my STL file to use these tools?

No. Every STLACCESS tool runs entirely in your browser. Your file is read locally with JavaScript — it is never sent to a server, never stored, and never seen by me. You can verify it yourself: open your browser's network tab while you use a tool and watch it stay empty.

Which STL formats are supported?

The STL Viewer and Printability Checker handle both binary and ASCII STL, the two encodings of the STL format. The STL Converter adds OBJ and PLY to that list. No installation is needed for any of them — a modern browser is enough.

Does the STL viewer work offline?

Yes, after the first page load. Because nothing is uploaded, all rendering happens on your own hardware. Once the page and its scripts are cached, you can disconnect from the internet and keep viewing and analyzing files. There is nothing to install and no account to create.

Is an STL file always in millimetres?

STL files carry no unit information at all — they are just numbers. Most slicers assume millimetres, but some exporters write inches. A file exported in inches imports 25.4× too small in a metric slicer. Checking the real dimensions before slicing is exactly what the Scale Inspector is for.

How do I check if my STL is watertight?

Use the STL Printability Checker. It flags open edges and non-manifold geometry — the two defects that make a slicer produce gaps or missing walls — in seconds, without uploading the file. Catching it before slicing saves a failed print, not just a re-slice.

Are these tools free, and do you track me?

All four tools are free with no account, no paywall, and no analytics on your files. The site is built and maintained by one person who has been 3D printing since 2017. If a tool saves you a failed print, supporting the site is optional and appreciated.

Why I built STLACCESS

I started 3D printing back in 2017 with a cheap entry-level FDM printer. In 2019, I ran a commercial print service in Enschede, Netherlands, but quickly realized running commercial queues drained the fun out of the hobby. I shut it down and returned strictly to hobby printing on a Bambu Lab A1 Mini.

Years of fixing mis-sized prints taught me one habit: verify the file before the machine commits hours and material to it. These four tools are that habit, generalized — the same checks I run at my own desk, turned into pages anyone can use without installing a thing.

Built, tested, and maintained by one person. Every tool runs in your browser, so I never see your files.
